Messages.Body:
So those of you who are going to Origins:

I'm thinking about running a Rapid Thought tournament on Friday night
after the Nationals. It would be pretty casual (if speedy) and I'd want
to keep it reasonably small (9-12 people including me as I have prize
support for that many people :-). The problem is that it would be:

A) After a day of playing VTES all day already.

B) Wouldn't start till, like, 10:00pm (although, as it would likely be
over by midnight anyway, that isn't a big deal).

The quick rundown of the rules is 45 minute rounds, 3 player games, Una,
Blood Doll, Minion Tap, Tribute, Vessel, and Villein are all banned.
Decks have minimum crypt size of 6 and should be 40-90 cards big. 3R+F.

Are there people who would want to be in on that crack wacky plan? If
so, let me know here.

I'll have a signup list near registration for the Nationals, and will
limit it to 12 people (I'm playing, and Kevin is probably playing, so
that makes room for 10 more). And it will cost a buck (as I have a
tournament support pack full of promos and some boosters for the winnar!)

And just to be clear, the whole point of Rapid Thought is to play the
most degenerate, mean, single minded brutal decks you can come up with.
'Cause everyone else will be doing that. So expect 2 caps with DOM and
weenie POT rush and anything else that is brutal and mean. And if you
get killed fast, it isn't a big deal, as the next game starts in 20
minutes anyway.

Yaa! So at Origins on Friday night, I ran a hilarious and wildly
successful Rapid Thought tournament. I planed on 12 people, but when
crunch time came, enough people were interested that we bumped it up
to 15 (5 tables of 3), which worked fine. We started a little after
10:00pm, and all 3 preliminary rounds were all done by midnight,
although in the third round, 2 games embarrassingly timed out (I kinda
wanna invent a new rule where if you are in a game that times out, you
lose all VPs to that point or something :-). The 3 player final was
done in about 40 minutes. Everyone seemed to have a good time, and the
decks were preposterous.

The final (and tournament) was won by my home town boy Dave Conroy
with a Jaroslav/2nd Tradition/Bundi deck. The final round was:

-Dave Conroy (see above)
-John Eno (weenie Animalism rush)
-David Litwin (protean rush)

Conroy got out Jaroslav early, and quickly found Jaroslav torpored due
to an unfortunate lack of fortitude meeting an unfortunate aggravated
hand strike, and then immediately diablerized, leaving Conroy kind of
a smoking crater. After that, Dave L and Eno beat the crap out of each
other, while Conroy influenced out his B-Team of Richter and Volker.
Eventually, after Dave L and Eno have eviscerated each other, Conroy
kind of poked them and they fell over, giving Conroy the 3VP sweep.

Again, the tournament was hilarious, wildly fun, and super quick (3R+F
done in less than 3 hours). Everyone should try this out.

-Peter

No problem! I love this format--again, I have no need for all of the
VTES tournaments I play to be this format, but the refreshingly quick
length (2-3 hours for the whole event) makes it so I can just organize
and run one at the drop of a hat, which is extra fun.

Yeah, I'm also still of the opinion that pool gain masters don't need to
be removed from the environment; I was in multiple games (and playing
with) where there were Voter Caps and Governs and Kindred Spirits which
added pool pretty quickly, and they didn't make a significant difference
in the length of the game (I was playing Voter Cap on pretty much every
vote I called, and the 10+ extra pool each game was mostly irrelevant to
the length of the game). These decks tend to be so focused that games
generally go where either:

A) Your deck works and you win!

or

B) Your deck doesn't, and someone else does!

Like, I was playing super degenerate 4 caps with PRE
KRC/Bewitching/VoterCap. In my first game, I was playing Kevin's Rock
Cat deck and RobbaYagga's Nocturn deck. My deck worked, Kevin's didn't,
and Robert's wasn't a deck that hurt mine too much. So I swept. Second
game, I was playing your deck and Greg's Dom/Aus deck. There was enough
reliable +1 intercept (as you have a couple birds, and Greg had Neighbor
John) that I think I only successfully called one vote the whole game
(and consequently, lost). Game 3 was me, Mark's Tremere IC deck and
Cameron's Caitiff Computer Hacking deck. I had to backoust Cameron (I
think I hit him with Anarchist Uprising, Neonate Breach, a 3 point KRC,
and the multiple 1 point KRCs before he died) and Mark drew into enough
dominate to kill me the turn where if he didn't kill me, I was certainly
killing him. In that game, pool gain masters probably would have helped
me and Mark live longer, but as the whole game took about 15 minutes, I
can't see that they would have made the game time out or anything.

And while I wasn't closely watching the two games that timed out (in the
same round), I don't think it was due to too much pool. It was due to
machination and general gridlock.

-A whole tournament is over in 2-3 hours.
-You can play the meanest, ugliest deck you can imagine, and it won't
result in "table hate", you won't "look like a threat", and no one is
going to gang up on you any more than they already were.

structure and short games, not having to work around the imposed
limits on deck building.

janky masters for pool gain (go King's Rising!), but I don't know that
that is worth compelling people to make special decks. But maybe it
is.

Peter D Bakija <pd...@lightlink.com> wrote:
>I mean, *I* like to make specific decks for the format and trying to
>specifically game the format, but that is me, and I don't expect that
>everyone is like that. And if folks are waffley about the format, and
>then they also have to make new decks?

Well, if you're all about getting people to try something new, you may
want to have a spare deck or six on hand.

As I see it, if people actually take to the Rapid Thought format
seriously[0], you're almost certainly going to find people tweaking
decks for it. Leaving aside all the possible bans you might or might
not make:

- you might change your bleed bounce a lot, because most of it will be
dead when you hit 2 players and My Enemy's Enemy probably becomes a
lot better

- Conservative Agitations pretty much all disappear from the game
(though they are found reasonably often in the TWDA)

- a variety of cards that generate table hate act faster and have fewer
people to go after you. e.g. there are two fewer players to try to
burn your Smiling Jack, and it goes up in value every third turn, not
every fifth...

- ... and for situations like this, your ratio of defensive cards to
other cards might change. (Since this cross-table guy isn't going to
blow up Jack, you need two fewer Wakes before you get to play your
next master card, say.)

- as a wall, Millicent Smith might be a much more interesting card
because it doesn't have that annoying period where it goes to my
grand-predator or grand-prey

- a combat deck may need much less bleed, because once one player is
ousted (which it can help with!), it just needs to demolish the other
player and can then bleed out happily and win fairly speedily.

- my Turbo deck only has to go off enough to beat two players. Perhaps
I can drop my total number of cards, and make hand jam less serious by
dropping from 80 cards to, say, 60.

Those sorts of considerations suggest to me that in a world where Rapid
Thought is a serious game format, players will already have to adapt
some of their decks reasonably significantly in order to have a good
chance of winning.

As a result, I don't think a different banned list is necessarily that
serious of an imposition on such players, *except* for when trying to
ensnare players to Rapid Thought in the first place. The burn option
suggestion seems to cover that reasonably well.

One thing I would be careful about, though, is how this format is
presented to new players. On the one hand, the 45 minute x 4 makes it
very attractive for conventions where you might demo it to other
players. On the other hand, the fact that the format is being presented
as (to paraphrase) play your nastiest possible deck and pound your
opponents into the dust may not make it the best introduction for new
players.

[0] e.g. using the 3 hour limit to make it pleasant to run at gaming
conventions.

--

I have a casual group that regularly plays 4 player games as well as
non Rapid Thought 3 player games, and aren't specifically treating our
games at tournament practice (i.e. we play 3 player games all the
time). I suspect that we play more 3-4 player games than 5 player
games (as we rarely have exactly 5, but often have 3-7). When we are
playing 3 and 4 player games, we do not enforce the maximum deck size
rule. When we play the occasional 6 player game, we also do not make
our decks 100 cards big.

-Peter
